title: How retail media platforms turn shoppers into ad revenue
summary: Retail media platforms let retailers sell advertising against their own shopper traffic, turning site visits, app sessions, and store trips into measurable media.
body_markdown:
Retail media platforms let retailers sell advertising against their own shopper traffic, turning site visits, app sessions, and store trips into measurable media. This guide covers ad formats, in-store and offsite expansion, first-party data targeting, auction mechanics, closed-loop reporting, build-versus-buy decisions, and what retail media networks look like through 2028.


## **Key takeaways on retail media platforms and shopper monetization**


- A retail media network is an advertising business a retailer runs against its own traffic, combining owned placements, shopper data, endemic and non-endemic demand, plus in-house measurement. Pharmacies, home improvement chains, delivery apps, and travel marketplaces run them too, and relevance often outweighs raw audience size.
- Sponsored products is the usual first launch among retail media ad formats because it is auction-priced, light on creative work, and easy to self-serve. Display, video, and in-store retail media follow once reporting history justifies CPM rates and proof-of-play logs can support billing.
- First-party data from transactions, loyalty records, and browse behavior powers targeting without third-party cookies, while contextual signals such as a live search query often convert well with no profile at all. Minimum audience sizes, consent handling, and clean rooms keep advertisers comfortable.
- Once onsite slots saturate, growth comes from offsite and connected TV (CTV) activation of retailer audiences measured back against sales. Closed-loop reporting is what attracts brand budget, though measuring return on ad spend (ROAS) honestly means separating attributed sales from incremental ones using holdout groups or geo experiments.
- The build-buy or hybrid decision hinges on traffic volume, engineering capacity, and existing demand relationships, and most retailers land on hybrid: owning identity and measurement while licensing ad serving. Pilot with a small cohort of supplier brands before publishing rate cards and expanding formats.


## **What a retail media network actually is and who runs one**


A[retail media network](https://perion.com/blog/what-is-retail-media-a-guide-with-basics-and-benefits/) is an advertising business operated by a retailer or marketplace that sells access to its shopper audience and its owned surfaces. The retailer controls the inventory, the data, and the measurement, which is what separates retail media from generic display advertising bought through the open web.


### **The core components**


- **Inventory:** search results pages, category and product detail pages, app placements, email, in-store screens, and offsite media bought on the retailer’s behalf.
- **Audience data:** logged-in purchase history, loyalty records, browse behavior, and cart activity.
- **Demand:** endemic brands that sell products on the retailer’s shelves, plus non-endemic advertisers buying access to the audience.
- **Measurement:** attribution that ties ad exposure back to transactions inside the retailer’s own systems.


### **Who operates these networks?**


The category started with large general merchandise and grocery chains, then expanded quickly. Pharmacy chains, home improvement retailers, convenience store groups, travel marketplaces, delivery apps, and even financial services companies now run comparable programs. Any business with authenticated users and transaction data has the raw material for a network.


Scale matters, but it is not the only requirement. A specialty retailer with a few million loyalty members and strong category authority can command meaningful CPMs because the audience is precisely the one its suppliers want to reach. Relevance frequently beats raw volume in pricing negotiations.


## **How retail media platforms turn shopper traffic into ad inventory**


The conversion from traffic to revenue follows a repeatable sequence. Retail media platforms sit between the storefront and the advertiser, deciding which commercial message appears in each available slot and at what price.


1. **Define placements.** Engineering teams carve out slots in search results, browse pages, checkout flows, and emails that can carry sponsored content without degrading the shopping experience.
2. **Connect the catalog.** The platform ingests product, price, and stock feeds so ads only serve for items that are actually purchasable and in stock.
3. **Open an auction.** Each impression triggers a bid request scored on bid value, product relevance, and expected click or conversion rate.
4. **Render and log.** The winning creative serves, and the impression, click, and any downstream order are written to a reporting pipeline.
5. **Bill and report.** Spend is reconciled against delivery, and advertisers see performance tied to real sales.


### **Why the economics work**


Retail media revenue carries far higher margins than product sales because the traffic already exists and the data is already collected. For many retailers, the incremental cost of an ad impression is close to zero after the platform is in place, which is why media income has become a meaningful contributor to operating profit at large chains.


The constraint is inventory discipline. Over-loading a search page with sponsored results lifts short-term revenue but damages conversion and trust. Mature networks set ad density caps, enforce relevance thresholds, and monitor organic conversion rate as a guardrail metric alongside media revenue.


## **Retail media ad formats that drive revenue in 2027**


Format mix determines both revenue ceiling and advertiser mix. Performance formats attract budget from trade and shopper marketing teams, while awareness formats pull from brand budgets that historically never touched retailer channels.


**Format** **Typical placement** **Pricing model** **Primary advertiser goal**


Sponsored products Search results, category pages, product detail pages CPC auction Direct sales and share of search


Sponsored brands Top of search, banner slots CPC or CPM Brand consideration plus traffic


Onsite display Homepage, browse, checkout CPM Awareness and new product launches


Onsite video App feeds, product pages CPM or CPV Storytelling near the purchase decision


Offsite social and display Third-party sites, social platforms CPM or CPC Reach beyond the retailer’s own traffic


In-store digital Entrance screens, aisle displays, self-checkout CPM or flat placement fee Influence at the point of selection


### **Which retail media ad formats to launch first**


Sponsored products are almost always the starting point. It has the clearest performance story, the lowest creative burden for advertisers, and it scales through self-service without a large sales team.[Display and video](https://perion.com/glossary/display-advertising/) follow once there is enough reporting history to justify CPM pricing.


Retailers with sizable catalogs should also consider sponsored listings in recommendation carousels and search autocomplete, which carry high intent and are rarely saturated. These placements often deliver strong click-through rates because they appear at the moment shoppers are narrowing their consideration set.


## **Scaling in-store retail media across physical locations**


[In-store retail media](https://perion.com/channels/in-store-retail-media/) extends the network into the environment where most retail spending still happens. The challenge is operational rather than technical: screens, audio, and shelf-edge devices live in thousands of locations with variable connectivity and local staffing.


### **Common in-store surfaces**


- **Entrance and welcome screens:** high-visibility, good for brand campaigns and seasonal pushes.
- **Aisle and endcap displays:** category-adjacent, strong for competitive conquesting and new item launches.
- **Self-checkout and register screens:** dwell time is predictable, which makes delivery forecasting easier.
- **Digital shelf labels and shelf-edge screens:** tie promotions directly to the product facing.
- **In-store audio:** inexpensive to deploy chain-wide and useful for reach-based packages.


### **Making in-store measurable**


Advertisers will pay premium rates only when store media is measured rather than estimated. Practical approaches include matching campaign flight windows against store-level sales lift, using holdout stores as a control group, and connecting loyalty card transactions to screens the shopper plausibly passed. Opportunity-to-see modeling based on traffic counters is standard for forecasting impressions.


Plan for the unglamorous parts: content scheduling by daypart and region, device health monitoring, proof-of-play logs for billing, and a creative spec that works across different screen sizes and orientations. Networks that skip proof-of-play run into disputes the moment a campaign underdelivers.

## **Pushing reach further with offsite and CTV inventory**


Onsite inventory is finite. Once the search page sells out, growth comes from taking retailer audiences off the property. Offsite and CTV campaigns use the retailer’s[first-party data](https://perion.com/glossary/first-party-data/) to target shoppers on social platforms, publisher sites, streaming services, and connected television, then measure the result back against retailer sales.


### **Why offsite expands the advertiser base**


- **Bigger budgets:** brand and media teams control larger pools of spend than shopper marketing.
- **Upper-funnel objectives:** reach and frequency goals that onsite placements cannot satisfy alone.
- **Non-endemic demand:** advertisers who sell nothing in the store but want the audience, such as automotive, travel, or financial brands.
- **Full-funnel narratives:** a CTV impression followed by an on-site sponsored product click, reported together.


### **CTV specifics**


Connected TV pairs well with retail data because household-level audiences map cleanly to household-level purchase records. The practical requirements are an identity bridge that can match retailer segments to streaming inventory without exposing raw customer data, frequency management across publishers, and incrementality testing so that CTV budget is not credited for sales that would have happened anyway.

The goal is one attribution framework across every surface, not separate reports per channel.


## **How first-party data powers targeting without third-party cookies**


The durable advantage of retail media is first-party data: authenticated, transaction-backed, and collected with a direct customer relationship. It does not depend on third-party cookies, which browsers and privacy settings have steadily restricted.


### **Data types and what they enable**


**Data type** **Example signal** **Targeting use**


Transactional Purchased a brand in the last 90 days Loyalty, replenishment, win-back


Behavioral Searched a category without buying Consideration-stage retargeting


Loyalty Tier, lifetime value, store preference High-value segments and regional targeting


Contextual Current page category or search term Intent targeting without any identifier


### **Governance is part of the product**


Brands will not fund a network they do not trust. Set rules before launch: minimum audience sizes to prevent re-identification, aggregated reporting rather than record-level exports, clear consent capture, honoring opt-outs across onsite and offsite activation, and contractual limits on how advertisers can reuse insights. Clean room environments let brands combine their own data with retailer data without either side seeing the other’s raw records.


Contextual targeting deserves more attention than it usually gets. Serving a sponsored product against a live search query requires no profile at all and often outperforms audience segments on conversion rate, which makes it a privacy-friendly default for a large share of inventory.


## **Auctions, pricing models, and yield management explained**


Pricing determines how much of the available value a network captures. Most onsite performance inventory runs on auction, while reserved placements and in-store packages are usually sold at fixed rates.


### **Auction mechanics**


- **Second-price style auctions:** the winner pays just above the next bid, which keeps bidding simpler for advertisers.
- **First-price auctions:** the winner pays the bid, which requires bid-shading tools and more experienced buyers.
- **Quality scoring:** blending bid with predicted click-through, relevance, and stock availability so the highest bidder does not automatically win with a poor match.
- **Floor prices:** category-level minimums that protect page quality and prevent underselling scarce inventory.


### **Pricing models in use**


CPC dominates sponsored products because it aligns cost with measurable traffic. CPM suits display, video, and in-store, where the objective is reach. Some networks offer cost-per-sale or ROAS-target bidding, which shifts risk toward the platform and demands reliable attribution. Flat-fee sponsorships still work for tentpole moments such as holiday hubs or category takeovers.


### **Yield levers**


1. Adjust ad density by page type based on measured impact on organic conversion.
2. Raise floors in categories with persistent excess demand.
3. Expand supply into under-monetized surfaces such as order confirmation pages and app notifications.
4. Use pacing controls so large advertisers do not exhaust inventory early in the month.
5. Package unsold in-store and offsite impressions with high-demand onsite slots.


## **Closed-loop reporting and measuring ROAS for advertisers**


[Closed-loop reporting](https://perion.com/blog/the-right-way-to-measure-media/) is the reason brands shift budget into retail media. Because the retailer observes both the ad exposure and the transaction, it can report sales attributed to a campaign without relying on third-party panels or modeled estimates.


### **What a credible report contains**


- **Delivery metrics:** impressions, clicks, viewability, and share of voice.
- **Attributed sales:** units and revenue within a stated lookback window.
- **ROAS:** attributed revenue divided by media spend, with the attribution rules spelled out.
- **New-to-brand metrics:** share of buyers who had not purchased the brand in a defined prior period.
- **Halo effects:** sales of the advertiser’s other items that followed exposure.


### **Why measuring ROAS needs context**


[Attributed ROAS](https://perion.com/glossary/return-on-ad-spend-roas/) is not incremental ROAS. A branded-keyword campaign will post an impressive number while capturing demand that existed anyway. Serious networks offer incrementality testing through holdout groups or geo experiments so advertisers can separate media-driven sales from baseline demand. Publishing the methodology, lookback windows, and attribution logic builds the trust that long-term budget commitments depend on.


Standardization efforts across the industry have pushed networks toward comparable metric definitions, which matters because brands buy across many retailers at once. Networks that report in line with recognized measurement guidelines make themselves easier to include in a planning cycle.


## **Build, buy, or hybrid decisions for retailers and marketplaces**


The build, buy, or hybrid question determines time to market, cost structure, and long-term control. There is no universally correct answer, only a fit against traffic volume, engineering capacity, and commercial ambition.


**Approach** **Time to launch** **Best suited to** **Main risk**


Build in-house Longest Very large retailers with mature engineering and data teams Sustained cost of ad tech roadmap and talent


Buy a platform Fastest Mid-size retailers wanting proven mechanics quickly Less differentiation and vendor dependency


Managed service Fast Retailers without a sales or ad ops organization Thinner margin, limited internal capability building


Hybrid Moderate Retailers that want to own data and identity while licensing delivery Integration complexity across owned and licensed components


### **Questions that settle the decision**


1. How much monetizable traffic exists today, and what revenue would a one to two percent ad load generate?
2. Can the engineering team maintain an auction, a forecasting system, and a billing pipeline alongside core commerce work?
3. Which components are genuinely differentiating, and which are commodity infrastructure?
4. Does the commercial team have relationships with brand budget holders, or is a partner needed for demand?
5. What happens to the data and advertiser contracts if the vendor relationship ends?


Hybrid is the common landing point. Retailers keep identity, audience definition, and measurement in-house, then license ad serving, auction logic, and offsite activation from specialists.


## **Evaluating vendors on reach, cost, integration, and support**


Vendor selection should be run like any enterprise software purchase, with weighted criteria and reference checks rather than a feature checklist alone.


### **Evaluation criteria**


- **Reach and demand:** which offsite channels the partner can activate, what CTV and digital out-of-home supply it accesses, and whether it brings existing advertiser relationships.
- **Format coverage:** sponsored products, display, video, in-store, and offsite in one system versus stitching together multiple tools.
- **Commercial model:** revenue share versus license fee, minimums, and how costs scale as spend grows.
- **Integration effort:** catalog and order feed requirements, identity resolution, SSO, API depth, and realistic engineering hours.
- **Measurement transparency:** documented attribution rules, incrementality tooling, clean room compatibility, and raw log access.
- **Support model:** named account team, onboarding help for advertisers, service levels, and roadmap influence.


### **Practical diligence steps**


Run a pilot on a limited set of categories before a full rollout. Ask vendors to demonstrate reporting against your own historical sales data rather than a canned demo environment. Speak with retailers of similar size, especially about what broke in the first six months. Confirm data residency and privacy terms with legal counsel early, since these frequently delay signature more than pricing does.


For[offsite and CTV](https://perion.com/blog/what-is-connected-tv-ctv-advertising-basic-explanation/) expansion in particular, favor partners with direct supply relationships and transparent fee structures across channels. ## **Launching your first campaigns and staffing the team**


A launch succeeds or fails on advertiser experience. The first cohort of brands will decide whether to renew based on how easy the network was to buy and how believable the reporting looked.


### **A workable launch sequence**


1. **Pilot:** 10 to 20 supplier brands across two or three categories, sponsored products only, with hands-on campaign management.
2. **Prove:** deliver clean reporting, gather feedback and document what advertisers actually ask for.
3. **Productize:** publish a rate card, creative specs, onboarding guide, and a self-service interface.
4. **Expand formats:** add display and video once there is enough performance history to justify CPM rates.
5. **Extend reach:** layer in in-store and offsite inventory, then sell full-funnel packages.


### **Roles to staff**


**Role** **Responsibility** **Hire timing**


Retail media lead P&L ownership, strategy, executive alignment Before pilot


Ad operations Trafficking, pacing, troubleshooting, proof of delivery Before pilot


Sales and account management Brand relationships, renewals, upsell into new formats Pilot to productize


Analytics and measurement Attribution, incrementality, reporting integrity Early, often shared with commercial analytics


Product and engineering Placement development, integrations, ad load governance Ongoing


Align incentives with merchandising from day one. If category managers see media revenue as competition for trade funds, the network stalls. Shared targets and joint business plans with suppliers keep both revenue streams growing instead of cannibalizing each other.


## **Where retail media platforms are headed through 2028**


The category is maturing from a handful of dominant networks into a wide field, which shifts the competitive pressure from existence to quality. Several directions look durable.


### **Trends worth planning for**


- **Measurement standardization:** continued convergence on shared metric definitions so brands can compare networks without manual normalization.
- **Growth in offsite and CTV:** onsite inventory saturates, so audience extension becomes the main growth lever for most networks.
- **In-store digitization:** more screens, retail audio, and shelf-level media, with better proof-of-play and sales-lift measurement.
- **Non-endemic demand:** advertisers outside the retailer’s own aisles buying access to high-quality shopper audiences.
- **Retail media networks as a service:** smaller retailers joining aggregated offerings instead of building independently.
- **Commerce beyond retail:** airlines, hotels, banks, telcos, and delivery platforms applying the same model to their own authenticated audiences.
- **AI in campaign operations:** automated bidding, creative variant generation, and anomaly detection reducing manual ad ops work.


### **What separates winners**


Networks that treat media as a shopper experience problem rather than a yield problem will hold their advertiser base. That means disciplined ad density, honest incrementality reporting, consistent measurement across onsite, in-store, and offsite surfaces, and a self-service product that a mid-size brand can actually use without an agency.


The underlying advantage does not change: a direct, consented relationship with shoppers and a complete record of what they buy. Retail media platforms that protect that relationship while making it easy for brands to buy will keep converting shopper traffic into durable, high-margin revenue.


## **FAQs about retail media platforms**


Common questions retailers and brands ask when planning or buying into a retail media network.


### **How much shopper traffic do you need before a retail media network makes sense?**


There is no fixed threshold. A useful test is to model what a modest ad load of one to two percent of impressions would earn at realistic CPCs, then compare that against platform and staffing costs. Specialty retailers with engaged loyalty bases often clear the bar on relevance rather than volume.


### **What is the difference between endemic and non-endemic advertisers?**


Endemic advertisers sell products on the retailer’s shelves, so their ads point straight at purchasable items and their budgets usually come from trade or shopper marketing. Non-endemic advertisers, such as banks, carmakers, or travel brands, sell nothing in the store but want access to the audience, typically funded from brand media budgets.


### **Will adding more sponsored placements hurt organic conversion?**


It can, which is why ad density needs a ceiling. Monitor organic conversion rate as a guardrail alongside media revenue, test density changes by page type, and enforce relevance thresholds so poorly matched ads cannot buy their way onto a page. Short-term yield gains are not worth lasting damage to shopper trust.


### **What is a data clean room and why do advertisers ask for one?**


A clean room is a controlled environment where a brand and a retailer can combine their datasets for analysis without either side seeing the other’s raw customer records. Brands ask for it because they want deeper audience and overlap insight than aggregated reports provide, while staying inside their own privacy commitments.


### **How long does it take to get from pilot to a self-service product?**


It depends on the approach. Licensing a platform or using a managed service shortens time to first campaign considerably, while building in-house takes longest. Most teams run a managed pilot with a handful of supplier brands first, then productize rate cards, creative specs, and self-service once reporting is proven reliable.


### **Who should own the media P&L inside the retailer?**


A dedicated retail media lead with clear P&L ownership, hired before the pilot, works best. Just as important is aligning with merchandising early. If category managers see ad revenue as competing with trade funds, the network stalls, so shared targets and joint business plans with suppliers are essential.
